evaluation.positioning_hook: A 1970s Christian zealot clones Jesus from the Shroud of Turin, then loses him to a stoned, confused 23-year-old who stumbles through modern Los Angeles before a rock-band crucifixion rescue mission kicks in.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly pitchable and has a clear comic engine, but the religious satire plus explicit sexual and drug material narrows the natural audience. It feels most marketable as cult-comedy or specialty genre fare rather than broad four-quadrant entertainment.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately: a fundamentalist group clones Jesus and then has to manage the consequences when the grown clone behaves like a confused modern kid. The opening pages set the premise fast and keep restating the central contradiction in new situations.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Wayne Bigsley, Jose, and Wendy Shapiro each have a playable comic angle, but they read more as satirical functions than deeply layered leads. Ted Nugent and Ross add color, though the script is more premise-driven than character-revealing.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to a blasphemous, absurdist premise and keeps escalating it through cloning, time travel, and rock-concert messianism. The willingness to mash biblical iconography, 1970s culture, and tabloid spectacle gives it a real signature.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: It moves with real comic propulsion: cloning announcement, birth, grown-up Jesus, time-machine retrieval, mistaken identity, and concert climax all keep the engine active. The middle does sprawl, but the story keeps resetting stakes in a way that sustains attention.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea is weird in a way that is also immediately legible: a zealot literally manufactures the second coming and then cannot control what Jesus does with modern culture. That combination of outrageous premise and simple emotional logic is the script’s strongest commercial asset.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is packed with specific satirical texture: televangelist fervor, lab science, 1970s corporate sponsorship, time-travel tech, and biblical reenactment all coexist. It’s not subtle, but it is story-generating and gives the script a lot of surfaces to play.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unmistakably irreverent, broad, and aggressively satirical, with a straight-faced commitment to absurdity. The script knows exactly what kind of joke it is telling and keeps the register consistent from the opening disco montage to the concert finale.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of a sharper satire about faith, spectacle, and cultural commodification, especially in Wayne’s obsession with control versus Jesus’ unpredictability. But the script mostly plays those ideas as comic premise rather than letting them deepen into a more layered emotional or thematic payoff.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Wayne/Shapiro/Ross form a workable comic triangle, and Jose’s dynamic with Wayne gives the script its main friction. Still, most supporting characters function as one-note satellites, so the ensemble energy is useful but not especially rich.

lead_characters.name: Wayne Bigsley
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 40s to early 50s, white, evangelical preacher, American
lead_characters.hook: The founder and true believer behind Jesus For a Peaceful Today, Wayne is a self-serious zealot with a salesman’s instinct for spectacle and a control freak’s terror of chaos. He wants the Second Coming, but only on his terms, and the comedy comes from watching his certainty collapse every time Jesus behaves like a person instead of a prophecy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Steve Carell in The Big Short or Jim Carrey in The Cable Guy — a comic lead who can play conviction, panic, and self-delusion in the same beat. It gives an actor a big, quotable role with room for escalating hysteria, moral vanity, and physical comedy.

lead_characters.name: Jose
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s, white-presenting, clone of Jesus Christ, physically youthful
lead_characters.hook: Jose is the cloned Jesus grown into a 23-year-old who has no interest in being a messiah and even less interest in the wardrobe, hair, or expectations forced onto him. He’s the movie’s wild card: half sacred icon, half reluctant stoner kid, and the source of the script’s best comic contradiction.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the deadpan innocence of Michael Cera in Juno while carrying the iconographic burden of a mythic figure. It offers a rare chance to play divine authority as baffled, youthful, and weirdly human.

lead_characters.name: Wendy Shapiro
lead_characters.hook: Wendy is the smartest person in the room and often the only one who can see the absurdity of what she’s helping build, which makes her both complicit and amused. She’s the script’s pragmatic counterweight: scientific, sensual, and just detached enough to keep the premise from floating away.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Sigourney Weaver in Ghostbusters or Kristen Wiig in Bridesmaids — a sharp, intelligent woman who can play straight-man authority while still landing the comedy. It gives an actor a role with wit, competence, and a sly erotic charge.

lead_characters.name: Ross Able
lead_characters.hook: Ross is Wayne’s loyal, dim, accident-prone right hand, forever trying to document the miracle while tripping over the machinery of it. He’s a classic comic follower: earnest, easily confused, and physically built for pratfalls.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that gives an actor the physical-comedy showcase of Chris Farley or John C. Reilly in a broad ensemble. It’s a role built on timing, innocence, and the ability to make repeated failure feel lovable.

lead_characters.name: Ted Nugent
lead_characters.hook: Ted Nugent arrives as a glorified action-comic guest star, all swagger, hair, and macho absurdity, and the script treats him like a weaponized personality. He’s not there for nuance; he’s there to blow darts, crash scenes, and turn the rescue mission into a rock-and-roll stunt.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of larger-than-life supporting turn that lets an actor do the Dennis Hopper in Blue Velvet thing — pure persona, maximum attitude, and instant scene theft. It’s a cameo-plus role with outsized comic visibility.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Larry James
lead_characters.hook: Dr. James is the dry, bureaucratic scientist who makes the time-machine insanity feel just plausible enough to keep moving. He’s the straight-faced technocrat in a movie full of zealots and lunatics, which makes him a useful comic anchor.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that plays like Jeff Goldblum in The Fly or John Lithgow in a comic-supporting mode — precise, slightly panicked, and funny because he treats the impossible as paperwork. It gives an actor a clean authority-comedy lane.

lead_characters.name: Genevieve
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s to 30s, white, lab biologist/botany consultant
lead_characters.hook: Genevieve is the sensual, willing vessel at the center of the cloning scheme, written as both sacred symbol and comic provocation. She’s less a fully individualized character than a charged presence who helps the movie push its blasphemous premise into motion.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the provocative, image-driven showcase of Sharon Stone in Basic Instinct or Jennifer Jason Leigh in a heightened genre part. It offers glamour, irony, and a knowingly outrageous premise hook.

lead_characters.name: Mary
lead_characters.hook: Mary is Jose’s mother and the script’s maternal reality check, forever trying to interpret divine events through the lens of ordinary parental concern. She’s a comic anchor in the biblical material, grounding the absurdity with practical worry.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play the warm, exasperated authority of a Diane Wiest or Frances Sternhagen type. It’s a compact but memorable mother role with strong comic timing.

lead_characters.name: Dwayne Bigsley
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 40s to 50s, white, religious leader, Wayne’s brother
lead_characters.hook: Dwayne is Wayne’s ideological mirror and family rival, giving the script a built-in split between competing religious factions. He’s mostly a pressure source, but the brother dynamic adds a useful personal edge to the larger satire.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a solid character-actor role in the vein of James Remar or J.K. Simmons playing institutional authority with a personal grudge. It gives an actor a chance to make a small amount of screen time feel like a real rivalry.

casting_characteristics: one principal lead with a strong comic monologue engine
period biblical roles plus contemporary Los Angeles roles
Ted Nugent and Charles Manson are named real-person portrayals

notable_requirements: biblical Jerusalem and related ancient-world sets
discotheque, church, lab, concert venue, time-machine room
crowd scenes for club, concert, street, and religious gatherings

technical.vfx_details: time-travel materialization, stylized transitions, and a few simple supernatural beats like walking on water and wall-passing Jesus
technical.sfx_needs: practical medical procedure setup, concert crowd choreography, dart/blowgun effects, simple miracle gags, smoke and lighting effects

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best positioned as a cult-comedy specialty title or streaming acquisition

budget.note: The script mixes contemporary Los Angeles with biblical Jerusalem, a time-machine set, concert staging, crowd scenes, and a few simple supernatural beats. It is not VFX-heavy, but the period split and music/concert footprint keep it above a lean contained-comedy cost profile.

casting.note: Wayne Bigsley has to carry the movie as a zealot, comic engine, and emotional straight man, while Jose needs to play Jesus as both icon and baffled young man. Ted Nugent, Dwayne Bigsley, and the biblical supporting roles add a lot of personality-specific casting pressure.

development.note: The premise is clear, but the script’s satire is broad and highly specific to its religious and pop-culture targets. Buyers will weigh whether the blasphemous comic register is a feature or a limiter for the intended audience.

comp_set.title: The Righteous Gemstones
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the same satirical appetite for religious spectacle, hypocrisy, and big comic behavior around faith.

comp_set.title: Dogma
comp_set.why_it_comps: A similarly irreverent religious-comedy lane built on theological provocation and pop-culture irreverence.

comp_set.title: Year One
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the broad, anachronistic biblical-comedy approach and the willingness to play scripture as absurdist farce.

comp_set.title: This Is the End
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the apocalyptic-comedy energy, celebrity-cameo texture, and escalation from hangout absurdity into end-times chaos.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like irreverent cult comedies, religious satire, and high-concept premise movies with a strong comic point of view.
audience_target.demographics: 18-49 skew, male-leaning but playable with women who respond to edgy satire; strongest with viewers comfortable with blasphemous humor and pop-culture parody.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary-plus-period feature with multiple crowd scenes, a concert climax, a time-machine set, and a modest amount of effects work.

types_of_buyers: mid-budget buyers open to edgy faith satire
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of irreverent, high-concept satire where the joke is the premise itself and the execution lives on comic confidence. The script’s mix of religion, rock music, and celebrity absurdity makes it a fit for buyers who want a conversation-starter rather than a broad crowd-pleaser.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the premise is built around a single escalation and does not present a clean sequel or spinoff vector.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one sentence, which is a real advantage in a crowded comedy market. That makes it easier to sell to specialty financiers, streamer comedy teams, and directors looking for a loud first- or second-feature calling card.
strengths.evidence: The opening cloning reveal and the 23-years-later payoff make the core engine unmistakable.

strengths.dimension_or_area: It has a genuine cult-comedy voice.
strengths.what_it_means: The script’s willingness to be sacrilegious, broad, and unembarrassed gives it a clear lane rather than a generic comedy tone. That kind of confidence is what cult buyers and midnight-movie audiences respond to.
strengths.evidence: The Manson opener, the cloning pitch, the rock-concert Jesus reveal, and the Ted Nugent rescue mission all commit to the same outrageous register.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Wayne Bigsley is a playable comic lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie has a central role that could attract an actor who wants a big, scene-stealing turn with physical comedy and moral panic. That is valuable packaging currency because the lead is not just functional; he is performative.
strengths.evidence: Wayne’s sermons, his panic over Jose, and his escalating attempts to control the situation drive the movie’s comic engine.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The biblical material is re-framed through modern absurdity.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the script a built-in contrast engine: sacred iconography colliding with contemporary slang, rock culture, and Los Angeles chaos. Buyers looking for a recognizable hook with a fresh wrapper will immediately get the appeal.
strengths.evidence: Jose’s confusion about hair, clubs, crack, and rock stardom keeps the biblical premise in a modern comic register.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The concert climax is a strong set-piece payoff.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie earns a big finale that can deliver crowd energy, music, and visual spectacle without needing tentpole-scale effects. That is useful for a mid-indie comedy because it gives the ending a memorable event shape.
strengths.evidence: The Greek Theater sequence with Jesus and the Hell Raisers turning into a gospel-rock spectacle is the script’s biggest crowd-pleasing swing.

whats_special.headline: This is a high-concept cult-comedy with a clean, pitchable engine and a lead role built for a fearless comic actor. The contained-to-moderate production footprint, plus the concert finale and celebrity-satire lane, make it the kind of specialty buy that can travel on premise alone.

items.area: The satire is broad enough to narrow the buyer pool.
items.detail: The script’s comic target is explicitly religious, and it leans hard into blasphemy, sexual humor, and drug material from the first pages onward. That makes the lane clear, but it also means the movie is naturally aimed at a narrower audience than a mainstream studio comedy.

items.area: The middle becomes episodic around the miracle beats.
items.detail: Once Jose is loose in modern Los Angeles and then in biblical Jerusalem, the script plays as a series of comic encounters more than a tightening escalation. The set-pieces are funny and distinctive, but a buyer will notice that the spine is premise-driven rather than pressure-driven for long stretches.

items.area: Jose reads more as a comic device than a full character.
items.detail: He is very effective as the baffled Jesus clone, but the page gives him less interiority than Wayne’s obsession or the premise itself. That is fine for a satire, but it limits the emotional range of the lead dynamic and keeps the movie from feeling more layered.

items.area: The rights and clearance list is not trivial.
items.detail: Charles Manson, Ted Nugent, Phillip Morris, Johnson and Johnson, Exxon, the NRA, Micron Labs, the Greek Theater, and named songs like "Brick House" and "Cat Scratch Fever" all create legal and business-affairs work. None of that is fatal, but it is real clearance and music-budget planning before greenlight.

issues.headline: The main friction is audience fit: the script knows exactly how far it wants to push, but that same aggressiveness makes it a specialty play rather than a broad one. Buyers will also clock the episodic middle and the non-trivial rights/music clearance list before they get to the upside.
